newsitem.title: USA: Calif. bill seeks to cut number of uninsured drivers.
newsitem.headline: Calif. bill seeks to cut number of uninsured drivers.

text.p: California's Legislature gave final approval late on Friday to a measure that would require California motorists to show proof of auto insurance every time they renew their vehicle registration.
State lawmakers said they backed the measure in a bid to reduce the number of uninsured drivers, who are blamed for a disproportionate share of accidents in the state.
California has long required drivers to carry auto insurance. The measure approved late on Friday would step up road-side enforcement of state auto insurance rules.
The bill permits police to check for insurance during stops for traffic infractions. Under current law, police may only check for insurance after an automobile accident.

A driver caught without insurance could pay a fine of $500 for a first offense and a $1,000 fine for a second offense under the new legislation, introduced by state Assemblywoman Jackie Speier, a Democrat.
The measure also would allow a court to impound uninsured vehicles for good cause.

State officials estimate that uninsured motorists in California cost insured motorists between $1 billion to $2.3 billion each year. Between 28 and 33 percent of all motorists are uninsured in California, state insurance officials said.

In other states that require drivers to provide proof of auto insurance to renew their registration and carry out road-side enforcement, the number of uninsured motorists has dropped dramatically, Speier said.
The Assembly approved the bill Friday night on a vote of 51-to-10, sending it to Gov. Pete Wilson, Speier's office said. The Senate approved the bill last year.
Critics of the bill say it unfairly targets uninsured drivers.
"We are criminalizing uninsured motorists instead of doing what we should do ... provide affordable auto insurance. This is a bad solution," state Assemblyman Antonio Villaraigosa, a Democrat, said.
